n: In this lesson we study food poisoning. The plan has seven stages. First we consider definition and classification: bacterial and non-bacterial types. Then bacterial poisonings, that is, toxicoinfection and intoxication, and then for botulism the clinical picture, changes in the body and diagnosis. After that poisonous mushrooms: death cap, false morel and fly agaric. Then alkaloids, potato and poisonous plants containing stones. Next, poisoning associated with fish and animals, additives and laboratory investigations are considered.

t: Section 1: definition and classification, in brief
n: The first section is devoted to definition and classification. Food poisoning, by circumstances, is regarded as an accident. We will answer short questions. Definition: the poisoning factor is present in the product or forms during preparation. A poison added from outside does not belong here. There are two main types: bacterial and non-bacterial. Bacterial types are toxicoinfection and intoxication. Non-bacterial types are associated with plants, animals and additives.

Food poisoning is usually associated with accidental circumstances. It includes the case where the poisoning factor is present in the composition of the product. It also includes the case where the factor formed during the process of preparation. Addition of poison from outside to ready food does not belong to this concept. This distinction must be known clearly.

Table 6.3 gives the classification of food poisoning. Poisoning is divided into bacterial and non-bacterial types. The bacterial type includes toxicoinfection and intoxication. The non-bacterial type is divided into three directions: poisoning associated with plants, with animals and with additives.

The second section briefly reviews bacterial poisoning. Here toxicoinfection and intoxication are distinguished. Toxicoinfection is associated with a product containing pathogenic bacteria. Intoxication is associated with a product in which toxin has accumulated. An important type is botulism. Another type is staphylococcal enterotoxin.

Let us consider toxicoinfection. Poisoning develops stormily and quickly. The causative agents are Salmonella and Escherichia coli. Products include meat, fish and milk, and sometimes also raw fruit and vegetables. In the clinical picture intoxication and dehydration are observed. The main syndrome is gastroenterocolitis.

We place toxicoinfection and intoxication side by side. In toxicoinfection, bacteria contaminate the product, poisoning develops rapidly, and dehydration and gastroenterocolitis occur. In intoxication, toxin has accumulated in the product. Toxins of microorganisms are accumulated; botulism is of particular importance, and staphylococcal enterotoxin also belongs to this group.

Botulism most often arises from home-prepared canned food. It belongs to the group of food intoxications. Products include canned mushrooms and vegetables, and also meat and fish products. The reason is that when the rules of preparation are violated, anaerobic microorganisms develop.

The clinical course of botulism develops stage by stage. The latent period lasts from hours to a day. Remember: the shorter the latent period, the more severe the disease. Then nausea, vomiting and constipation appear. Then vision is disturbed. Finally bulbar paralysis and disturbance of breathing develop.

In botulism, ocular signs and bulbar paralysis are distinguished separately. In visual disturbance there are mydriasis, ptosis and diplopia, paresis of accommodation develops, and the light reaction is lost. In bulbar paralysis, paralysis of the soft palate, pharynx and larynx is observed. The voice is lost, which is called aphonia, and swallowing becomes difficult. Disturbance of breathing is linked with the diaphragm and the respiratory centre.

Death from botulism usually occurs on the second day, sometimes later. The cause is paralysis of the respiratory centre. In the body mild gastroenteritis and degeneration of parenchymatous organs are found. Acute change of neurons is also identified. In histology the nuclei of the cranial nerves are altered.

Diagnosis of botulism rests on three supports. The first is the clinical picture, that is, clinical signs. The second is biological examination: botulinum toxin is detected in animals. The third is sanitary-hygienic examination, that is, examination of food remnants. These three directions together substantiate the diagnosis.

Staphylococcal enterotoxin is also a type of bacterial poisoning. The cause is staphylococcal enterotoxins. It most often arises from contaminated dairy products. In the clinical picture gastroenteritis and intoxication are observed. The outcome is good: with treatment, recovery within a few days.

t: Procedure in death from bacterial poisoning
n: The procedure in death from bacterial poisoning is as follows. If the diagnosis has clinical and laboratory confirmation, a pathological-anatomical examination is carried out. If the diagnosis is not confirmed, a forensic examination is ordered only if violent death is suspected. In that case a forensic medical examination is carried out.

The third section is devoted to non-bacterial poisoning. It has three groups: plant, animal and additive. Poisoning associated with plants includes poisonous mushrooms and poisonous plants. Poisoning associated with animals includes fish and secretory glands. Poisoning associated with additives includes chemicals, weeds and fungi.

We compare the most frequently encountered poisonous mushrooms. The death cap contains amanitotoxin, poisoning begins in 6–24 hours, mortality 50–70 %. In the false morel the toxin is gyromitrin acid, onset 6–10 hours, mortality about 30 %. The fly agaric contains muscarine and other substances, signs appear within 6 hours, and death is rare.

The toxins of the death cap are amanitotoxin, phalloidin and others. Amanitotoxin is not destroyed by heat treatment. They cause destruction in the central nervous system, liver and kidney. The clinical picture begins after 6–24 hours and runs like cholera. Mortality is 50–70 %, and death occurs in 2–3 days. In the body, haemorrhages and fatty degeneration are found.

The toxin of the false morel is gyromitrin acid. It is unstable to drying. The action is haemolytic and hepatotropic. The clinical picture begins after 6–10 hours: haemolysis and hepatitis develop. Mortality is about 30 %, and death occurs in 3–4 days. In the body jaundice and small haemorrhages are found.

The fly agaric has three toxic substances. Muscarine is a cholinomimetic and is regarded as an atropine antagonist. Muscaridine has an atropine-like cholinolytic action. Pilztoxin is a convulsant substance. The clinical picture depends on the species of mushroom.

In muscarine poisoning death is rare; in severe cases it occurs on the first day. First the pulse quickens and the pupil constricts. Then vomiting and abdominal pain appear. Then the central nervous system is stimulated, and afterwards depressed. Finally delirium and disturbance of consciousness are observed.

The fourth section is devoted to poisonous plants. This poisoning occurs mainly in the warm months of the year. The person consumes the fruit, stem or root. There is no characteristic change in the body; signs of rapid death are observed. Diagnosis rests on the circumstances, clinical picture and forensic chemistry. In addition, botanical examination is carried out.

The clinical picture of poisonous plants depends on the action of alkaloids. Monkshood, in Latin Aconitum, contains aconitine. Hemlock, Conium maculatum, contains coniine. Water hemlock, Cicuta virosa, contains cicutoxin. Belladonna, thorn apple and henbane contain atropine, scopolamine and hyoscyamine.

The poison of monkshood is aconitine. The lethal dose is 0.004–0.005 g. Mechanism of action: persistent depolarisation of the membrane, sodium permeability is disturbed, and the action passes to the central nervous system and the conducting system of the heart. Signs: pain and itching in the mouth and pharynx, profuse saliva, the pupil constricts. There are convulsions, tachycardia, then bradycardia. Consciousness is preserved and collapse develops.

Hemlock contains coniine, which acts like nicotine. The plant is mistaken: its leaves resemble parsley and its root horseradish. Signs: burning in the mouth, saliva and vomiting. Paralysis begins in the legs and ascends. The lethal dose is 0.5–1.0 g.

Cicuta, that is, water hemlock, grows on the banks of water and in marshes. The root is spongy and sweet, so it is eaten by mistake, being taken for celery. Signs begin in a few minutes. In the clinical picture there are vomiting, bradycardia and clonic convulsions. Death occurs from paralysis of the respiratory muscles.

Plants of the atropine group contain M-cholinolytic alkaloids: atropine, scopolamine and hyoscyamine. Poisoning begins with dry mouth and a burning sensation. Then the face reddens and drowsiness appears. The pupil dilates. Finally acute psychosis develops, and death occurs from paralysis of the respiratory centre.

Let us consider solanine in potato. In greened potato, solanine is 6–10 times greater. Normally its amount is 0.001–0.003 %. In sprouted, greened potato it is 0.02–0.03 %. In the clinical picture acute gastroenteritis is observed.

Poisoning is possible when kernels of the stones of unripe fruit are eaten in quantity. The stone kernel contains amygdalin. Under the action of gastrointestinal enzymes hydrocyanic acid is formed from it. As a result poisoning develops. Remember the chain in this order.

t: Section 5: the animal world, in brief
n: The fifth section is devoted to the animal world. The eggs of fish, that is, roe, and milt may be poisonous. In southern seas the neurotoxin tetrodotoxin occurs. Animal glands are also a cause of poisoning: pancreas, adrenal and testis. The condition is incomplete heat treatment.

In fish poisoning, tetrodotoxin is a strong neurotoxin. Of local fish, the roe and milt of the marinka, “suzanbalik” and “qorabaliq” are poisonous. In southern seas needlefish and dog-like fish are dangerous. Their roe, milt, liver, intestine and skin are poisonous. Here, under the action of tetrodotoxin, more than half die.

In the clinical picture of fish poisoning, signs from the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system come together. In the gastrointestinal tract there are nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. In the central nervous system weakness, headache and myalgia appear. Paraesthesia, ataxia, aphonia and dysphagia are observed. Convulsions also occur.

Let us consider poisoning with animal glands. The glands: pancreas, adrenal and testis. The animals: cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. The cause is incomplete heat treatment. The clinical picture consists mainly of signs characteristic of gastroenteritis.

The sixth section briefly considers poisonous additives. This poisoning has a group character: it is linked with a family, a ceremony or a locality. Sources: seed grain and potato treated chemically, weeds, that is, heliotrope and Trichodesma (“kampirchopon”). Also fungi: fusariosis and ergotism. The investigation is also epidemiological.

Let us consider the consequences of grain and weed additives. The clinical picture depends on the active substances in the additive. Poisonous chemical treatment gives signs that depend on the substance. Heliotrope causes chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis of the liver. Trichodesma (“kampirchopon”) leads to toxic encephalitis. Grain fungi cause mycotoxicosis: fusariosis and ergotism.

In group poisoning the investigation is multi-directional. The group character is linked with a family, a group of people, that is, a ceremony, or the population of a locality. Investigations: clinical and morphological, forensic chemical and epidemiological. That is, clinical, morphological, forensic chemical and epidemiological methods are applied together.

The seventh section is devoted to laboratory investigations. They are carried out to prove or exclude poisoning. Forensic chemical and histological examination are the most frequently used. Histology determines microscopic changes. Results are assessed together with other data.

In the table we see which examination is needed for which poisoning. For biologically active plants, botanical examination. For mushrooms, mycological examination. For metal-containing substances, physical, that is, spectral, examination. For food poisoning, bacteriological and biological examination. For substances acting on enzymes, biochemical examination. The choice follows from the features of the incident.

t: False positive and false negative results
n: Let us speak about false positive and false negative results. Results are always assessed together with other information. No poison, but it is found: the substance was used as a medicine, formed in putrefaction, is linked with occupational activity, or there were deficiencies in sampling. Poison present, but not found: the substance broke down rapidly, intensive infusion therapy was given, more time has passed, or the method has not yet been developed.

t: Taking samples in a medical institution
n: Let us consider the procedure for taking samples in a medical institution. Objects are taken as quickly as possible. Main samples: blood and urine. Additional objects: gastric lavage fluid, vomit and faeces. If remnants of the poison, its container or packaging are brought with the victim, these are also taken. All is sent to the toxicology laboratory.

The first teaching case. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: home-prepared canned food was eaten. After several hours vomiting and dry mouth appeared. Vision was disturbed: mydriasis and ptosis. Then swallowing is difficult and there is no voice. Questions: which type of poisoning? Why is it dangerous? How is it confirmed?

The answer to the first case. The signs correspond to botulism. Type: botulism, a food intoxication. It is dangerous because of paralysis of the respiratory muscles and centre. Condition of the cause: anaerobic growth in the canned food. For confirmation, the clinical picture and biological examination on animals are needed. In addition, sanitary examination of the food remnants is carried out.

The second teaching case is also hypothetical, not a real examination. Given: gathered mushrooms were eaten. After 6–24 hours cholera-like signs appeared. On days 2–3 renal failure developed. In the body fatty degeneration and haemorrhages were found. Questions: which mushroom is likely? Which toxin? Which examination is needed?

The answer to the second case. The signs correspond to death cap poisoning. The toxin is amanitotoxin, resistant to heat treatment. Examination: mycological, and also forensic chemistry and histology. Mortality is 50–70 %, and the cause is acute renal failure.

Let us gather the main points of support of the lesson. Food poisoning, by circumstances, is an accident. Bacterial poisoning is divided into toxicoinfection and intoxication. Botulism is characterised by canned food, visual disturbance and bulbar paralysis. In mushrooms the clinical picture differs according to the type of toxin. In poisonous plants there is no characteristic change in the body; botanical examination and forensic chemistry are needed. Additives have a group character, and epidemiology is applied.

The review questions rest on pp. 172–181 of the chapter. First question: what are the types of food poisoning? Second: what do the clinical picture and diagnosis of botulism consist of? Third: what is the difference between the death cap and the false morel? Fourth: what do you know about aconitine, coniine and cicuta? Fifth: list the causes of false results.
